paper_context.research_question: Can unannotated grammatical error correction (GEC) system output be automatically annotated with edit spans and dataset-agnostic error-type labels accurately enough to enable per-error-type evaluation of system performance?
main_claims: A linguistically-enhanced alignment combined with a dataset-independent rule-based classifier can automatically extract edits between original and corrected sentences and assign error-type labels without requiring annotated training data.
Human experts rated the automatically predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable' in at least ~95% of cases in a small-scale manual evaluation, indicating high qualitative appropriateness.

Auto-annotating both hypotheses and references and evaluating with the proposed edit-comparison approach yields results comparable (no significant difference by bootstrap testing) to evaluation using gold references and standard M2 scoring.

Applying this automatic annotation enables the first detailed per-error-type analysis of CoNLL-2014 system outputs, revealing complementary strengths and weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT systems better at multi-token and certain noun errors; classifiers better at some verb-form and orthography errors).
The rule-based, deterministic classifier is transparent and dataset-independent, avoiding dataset-specific biases of learned classifiers.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Annotation accuracy/appropriateness of predicted error types (human judgment distribution Good/Acceptable/Bad; inter-annotator agreement κfree).
Robustness of edit extraction (alignment quality measured indirectly via downstream labeling and comparison to gold references).
Comparability with existing evaluation metrics (differences vs. M2 scorer and statistical significance testing).
Coverage and granularity of the proposed error taxonomy (number of types, ability to prefix with M/R/U tiers).
Utility in diagnostic analysis (ability to reveal per-system strengths/weaknesses, multi-token edit performance, detection vs correction).
Dependence on upstream NLP tools (POS tagging, lemmatization, parsing, stemming, and spellcheckers) and error sensitivity caused by their mistakes.
Generalisability to other datasets and languages (dataset-independence claim tempered by reliance on specific automatic mark-up quality).

extracted_claims.claim_text: Edit spans between original and corrected sentences are automatically extracted using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) with merging rules, which approximates human edits effectively and is used as the edit-extraction component in this work.
evidence: Section 2: "we use [Felice et al. (2016)] ... a linguistically-enhanced alignment supported by a set of merging rules."
Section 2: "This approach ultimately proved most effective at approximating human edits in several datasets (80-85 F1), and so we use it in the present study."
uncertainty_flags: Reported 80-85 F1 refers to Felice et al. (2016) results, not a new evaluation on the CoNLL-2014 data within this paper.
No direct quantitative breakdown of alignment errors on the CoNLL-2014 hypotheses is provided in the manuscript.

extracted_claims.claim_text: A deterministic, dataset-independent, rule-based classifier that uses only automatic mark-up (POS, lemma, stem, dependency parse, spellcheck) can assign error-type labels to extracted edits without requiring annotated training data.
evidence: Section 3: "we wrote a rule to classify an edit based only on its automatic POS tags... ensured that all types are assigned based only on automatically obtained properties of the data."
Section 3.1: "prerequisites ... POS tagged, lemmatized, stemmed and dependency parsed. We use spaCy v1.6 ... Lancaster Stemmer ... Hunspell GB-large..."
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which the rule set covers edge cases is not quantitatively described beyond the manual rating sample.
Performance dependence on the chosen versions/configurations of external tools (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) is asserted but not systematically tested.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The proposed framework defines 25 (plus operation-tier prefixes leading to 55 possible codes) error types, which can be prefixed with operation tiers M:, R:, U: to allow varying granularity of evaluation.
evidence: Section 3.2: "The complete list of 25 error types in our new framework is shown in Table 2... can be prefixed with ‘M:’, ‘R:’ or ‘U:’..."
Appendix A / Table 9: detailed listing of token/operation/morphology tiers and combinations; mentions 55 total possible error types.
uncertainty_flags: Choice of categories (e.g., treating modal+tense as tense) is motivated by practicality; alternate granular taxonomies could change labeling.
No inter-annotator taxonomic validation besides manual rating of predicted labels is provided.

extracted_claims.claim_text: In a small-scale manual evaluation, five GEC researchers rated 200 randomly chosen automatically predicted edits (100 FCE-test, 100 CoNLL-2014) and each rater considered at least 95% of predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable'; overall distribution across raters was 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad, with κfree = 0.724.
evidence: Section 3.3: description of 5 raters, 200 edits sample, rating scheme Good/Acceptable/Bad.
Table 3: per-rater percentages and overall 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad; inter-annotator agreement 0.724 κfree (Randolph, 2005).
uncertainty_flags: Sample size is small (200 edits) and may not represent full variety of edits or error types present in CoNLL-2014 system outputs.
Raters were instructed to focus on category appropriateness despite automatically determined boundaries, which may mask boundary-related classification errors.

extracted_claims.claim_label: POS tagger errors cause most 'Bad' labels
extracted_claims.claim_text: When raters judged predicted categories as 'Bad', these errors could usually be traced back to mistakes by the POS tagger (e.g., ambiguity leading to NOUN:NUM vs VERB:SVA confusion).
evidence: Section 3.3: "whenever raters judged an edit as 'Bad', this could usually be traced back to a mistake made by the POS tagger; e.g. [ring → rings] might be considered a NOUN:NUM or VERB:SVA error depending on whether the tagger considered both sides of the edit nouns or verbs."
uncertainty_flags: No quantitative breakdown of 'Bad' cases by underlying NLP-tool error type is provided—claim based on observed examples.
POS tagger version and error rates on learner data are not fully reported, so extent of this effect across dataset is uncertain.

extracted_claims.claim_label: auto reprocessing references matches gold evaluation
extracted_claims.claim_text: Reprocessing gold reference edits automatically (running alignment+classifier on references) and then evaluating hypotheses against these auto-annotated references yields overall scores that are not significantly different from evaluation using gold references and the M2 scorer (bootstrap testing, 1000 iterations, p > .05).
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 4.1 (Gold Reference vs. Auto Reference), Table 4
evidence: Section 4.1: explanation of reprocessing references to align evaluation setups, and statement: "We validated this hypothesis for each team by means of bootstrap significance testing (1,000 iterations, p > .05)."
Table 4: side-by-side M2 scorer and 'Our Approach' scores for Gold and Auto references for teams.
uncertainty_flags: Exact statistical test details (e.g., which metric tested, confidence intervals, exact p-values per team) are not fully reported.
Table 4 shows differences in absolute numbers; the claim relies on the bootstrap test but per-type or per-team non-significant differences may mask category-specific discrepancies.

extracted_claims.claim_text: If hypothesis and reference files are annotated in the same format, a simple edit-comparison approach (matching edits by span and correction) can be used to compute precision/recall/F-score at the edit level; this approach treats edit extraction and evaluation as separate tasks.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 4 (CoNLL-2014 Shared Task Analysis), Section 4 intro
evidence: Section 4: "if both the hypothesis and reference files are annotated in the same format, we need only compare the edits in each file to produce an F-score... any edit with the same span and correction in both files is a true positive..."
Section 4: "Our approach... treats edit extraction and evaluation as separate tasks."
uncertainty_flags: Matching requires identical spans and corrections; partial matches or semantically equivalent multi-edit decompositions may be counted as mismatches (authors note such cases).
No formal analysis of sensitivity to span granularity or alternative matching strategies is given.

extracted_claims.claim_label: M2 scorer tends to overestimate performance
extracted_claims.claim_text: The M2 scorer tends to overestimate system performance compared to the authors' edit-comparison approach because M2 exploits dynamic edit boundary selection to maximize true positives and minimize false positives.
evidence: Section 4.1: discussion and examples where M2 chooses multi-edit decompositions or merges FPs within a distance to maximize TPs, leading to higher scores; "M2 scores tend to be higher than our own... M2 scorer in fact tends to overestimate performance."
uncertainty_flags: Claim illustrated by examples but no comprehensive quantitative comparison across edit types or systems is provided beyond Table 4 aggregate differences.
Degree of overestimation may depend on M2 settings (e.g., max unchanged words parameter) and dataset characteristics.

extracted_claims.claim_label: first per-error-type analysis of CoNLL-2014 systems
extracted_claims.claim_text: Auto-annotating hypotheses and references enables a detailed per-error-type analysis of all CoNLL-2014 system outputs, revealing complementary strengths and weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT systems better at multi-token and certain noun errors; classifiers better at some verb-form and orthography errors).
evidence: Section 4: authors applied tool to all teams' outputs and present per-team per-type precision/recall/F0.5 tables (Tables 5, 6, 7, 8) and narrative summarising strengths (e.g., CAMB best in 10 categories, CUUI strong in ORTH and VERB:FORM).
Section 4.5: multi-token edit performance table (Table 8) shows MT systems higher on multi-token edits.
uncertainty_flags: Analysis depends on the correctness of automatic edit extraction and classification; propagation of upstream errors could bias per-type findings.
Statistical tests for whether inter-system per-type differences are significant are not consistently reported.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The automatic annotation tool used in this study will be released with the paper.
evidence: Abstract: "The tool we use to do this will be released with this paper."
Section 1 and Section 5 repeat that the tool will be released.
uncertainty_flags: No URL, license, or release date is provided in the manuscript itself; actual availability needs verification outside the paper.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) performs adequately on learner and system-generated text such that extracted edit spans correspond closely enough to human-intended edits for downstream error typing and evaluation.
supporting_evidence: Adoption of Felice et al. (2016) method and citation of 80-85 F1 on several datasets.
Manual classifier evaluation asks raters to ignore boundary oddities but asserts high label appropriateness.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If alignment frequently produces incorrect or inconsistent spans, then classifier labels (even if correct for the wrong span) will mismatch references and evaluation F-scores will be misleading; per-type analyses may be biased.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Automatic NLP preprocessing tools (spaCy v1.6 for POS/lemma/parse, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) produce sufficiently accurate annotation on noisy learner language and diverse system outputs to support reliable rule-based classification.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.1 specifies the toolchain and mapping to UD POS tags.
Section 3.3 notes POS tagger mistakes account for many 'Bad' ratings.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Tool errors (POS, lemma, parse, stemming, spellcheck) can systematically misclassify edits, inflate 'Good' ratings in limited samples while causing biased per-type metrics across larger datasets.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Manual rating of 200 edits by 5 experts is representative of overall classifier accuracy/appropriateness across datasets and error types.
supporting_evidence: Manually rated sample: 200 edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL-2014), 5 raters, reporting percentages and κfree.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the sample is not representative (bias toward easier or more common edits), the reported high appropriateness may overstate true label quality; downstream per-type evaluation could be unreliable for rarer or more complex error types.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Reprocessing gold references with the same automatic alignment and classifier removes mismatches sufficiently so that comparisons between auto-annotated hypotheses and auto-annotated references are fair proxies for gold-based evaluation.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 4.1 (Gold Reference vs. Auto Reference), Table 4
supporting_evidence: Authors report bootstrap testing showing no significant difference between auto and gold references (1,000 iterations, p > .05) and present Table 4 comparing M2 and their approach with gold/auto.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If reprocessing introduces systematic distortions (e.g., merging/splitting edits differentially), claiming equivalence to gold evaluation could be incorrect and per-team or per-type results could be skewed.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Matching edits by identical span and correction is an adequate evaluation criterion for measuring system performance at the error-type level.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 4 (CoNLL-2014 Shared Task Analysis), Section 4 intro
supporting_evidence: Section 4: description of matching criteria and use to compute TP/FP/FN for evaluation.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: This strict matching can undercount semantically equivalent corrections split across multiple edits or with different span choices, potentially penalising systems that correct at different granularities or produce equivalent but differently segmented edits.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Differences between M2 scoring and the authors' edit-comparison approach reflect M2's tendency to exploit dynamic boundaries, not errors in the authors' approach.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.1: explanation with examples of M2 preferring decomposed edits and merging nearby FPs, leading to higher M2 scores.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the authors' method also under- or over-counts in systematic ways, attributing all differences to M2's bias could be misleading; comparative conclusions about relative system performance might be affected.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Per-error-type F0.5 scores computed from auto-annotated hypotheses and references reflect true differences in system capabilities and are not dominated by annotation or alignment artifacts.
supporting_evidence: Detailed per-type tables and narrative attributing strengths to approaches (MT vs classifiers) are presented as meaningful.
Authors note some observed failures tied to system design (e.g., missing unnecessary token corrections).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If annotation/alignment errors vary by error type (e.g., some types are harder to align or tag), the per-type performance differences might reflect tooling limitations rather than true system competence.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The taxonomy's granularity (25 base types, 55 with operation prefixes) is practical and sufficient for diagnostic evaluation without causing excessive misclassification or ambiguity.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.2: authors discuss compromise between informativeness and practicality and give examples about modal vs tense treatment decisions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Insufficient granularity could conflate distinct error phenomena; excessive granularity could increase classifier mistakes and reduce reliability of per-type metrics.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The toolchain choices (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell GB-large) are sufficiently language- and domain-appropriate for the English learner texts in CoNLL-2014 and FCE-test.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.1 lists the tools used but does not provide empirical validation of their suitability on these corpora within the paper.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Toolchain mismatches (e.g., stemmer behavior, spellcheck dictionary variants) may produce systematic labeling errors, particularly for non-standard learner orthography or rare forms.

argument_focus: Demonstrate that deterministic, rule-based, dataset-agnostic annotation of edits enables per-error-type evaluation of unannotated GEC outputs.
Show that auto-processing of both hypotheses and references yields comparable evaluation results to gold references when using consistent processing.
Provide a taxonomy and operationalization (M/R/U tiers) that supports multi-granularity diagnostic analyses.
contribution_targets: A reusable tool and pipeline for automatic edit extraction and dataset-independent error-type labeling for English GEC datasets (implemented with specified NLP toolchain).
A compact error taxonomy for GEC with operation-tier prefixes enabling token- and operation-level analyses.
An empirical per-system diagnostic analysis of CoNLL-2014 systems using the auto-annotation pipeline.
evaluation_targets: Validity of the alignment and edit-extraction method on system outputs (span correctness, merging/splitting behavior).
Robustness of rule-based classifier labels across error types, toolchain variants, and larger representative samples beyond the 200-edit manual test.
Equivalence of auto-processed references to gold references across aggregate and per-type metrics (statistical test details, effect sizes).
Sensitivity of per-type performance results to preprocessing errors (POS/tagging/lemmatization/stemming/spellcheck).
Impact of strict span+correction matching on evaluation of multi-token and decomposed edits (false negatives from segmentation differences).
uncertainty_flags: Small manual evaluation sample (200 edits) limits generalisability of reported >95% Good/Acceptable rates.
POS/tagging and alignment errors are acknowledged but not exhaustively quantified across the full CoNLL-2014 outputs.
Bootstrap testing claim (p > .05) lacks full reporting of test statistic, per-team p-values, and which metrics were tested.
Tool release is promised but no artifact URL or versioning details are given in the manuscript.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should (a) test alignment/span quality empirically on a larger sample of CoNLL-2014 system outputs, (b) quantify classification errors by error type and correlate them with upstream POS/lemma/parse/spellcheck mistakes, and (c) re-run statistical comparisons to gold references with full reporting (p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes) and per-type analyses.

When assessing per-system claims of strengths/weaknesses, reviewers should control for annotation/alignment artifacts by inspecting a stratified sample of matched and unmatched edits, and consider alternative matching strategies (e.g., fuzzy span matching, semantic equivalence) to measure sensitivity.
If possible, reviewers should attempt the pipeline with alternate preprocessing tool versions (modern spaCy, different stemmer, updated dictionaries) to measure dependency on toolchain choices.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a pipeline for automatically extracting edit spans between original and corrected sentences using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) and classifying those edits with a deterministic, rule-based, dataset-agnostic taxonomy (25 base types; 55 with operation prefixes). The authors manually validate label appropriateness on a small sample (200 edits, 5 expert raters), report high qualitative ratings (≈86% Good, 10% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad; κfree=0.724), and then apply the tool to all CoNLL-2014 system outputs to produce per-error-type precision/recall/F0.5 analyses. They also show that reprocessing references automatically yields aggregate scores not significantly different from gold-reference evaluation (bootstrap testing, 1,000 iterations, p>.05), and argue that this auto-annotation enables first detailed per-error-type diagnostics revealing complementary strengths of different system approaches. The argument chain is coherent but relies on several operational assumptions (alignment quality, NLP preprocessing reliability, and representativeness of a small manual sample). Key weaknesses are limited quantitative error analysis of alignment/classifier failures across full datasets, sparse reporting of statistical test details, and potential sensitivity of per-type results to upstream tool errors and strict exact-span matching.
logical_argument_graph: P1: System outputs in GEC are typically unannotated for error type; per-type evaluation is therefore impossible (Intro).
P2: Accurate per-error-type evaluation requires reliable edit-span extraction and type assignment (Intro → Edit Extraction + Typing).
P3: Felice et al. (2016) linguistically-enhanced alignment approximates human edits well (reported 80–85 F1), so using it for edit extraction is reasonable (Section 2).
P4: A deterministic rule-based classifier using only automatic markup (POS, lemma, parse, stem, spellcheck) can be dataset-agnostic and transparent (Section 3).
P5: Small-scale manual validation shows predicted types are judged Good/Acceptable in ≈96% of sampled cases, implying high qualitative appropriateness (Section 3.3).
C1: Therefore, automatically extracting edits and assigning dataset-independent error types is feasible and yields qualitatively appropriate labels for many edits (from P3+P4+P5).
P6: If both hypotheses and references are auto-annotated with the same pipeline, edit-level comparison via exact span+correction matching can compute precision/recall/F (Section 4).

P7: Reprocessing gold references with the same automatic pipeline yields aggregate scores not significantly different from gold-based M2 scoring (bootstrap p>.05), so auto-refs are a fair proxy at aggregate level (Section 4.1 + Table 4).
C2: Thus, the pipeline enables fair comparative evaluation of system outputs without needing manual reference re-annotation (from P6+P7).
P8: Applying the pipeline to all CoNLL-2014 systems yields per-type metrics that reveal complementary strengths/weaknesses across approaches (Sections 4.2–4.6, Tables 5–8).
C3: The auto-annotation tool therefore enables novel diagnostic insights into system behavior (from P8).

Critical dependencies/risks: Alignment errors, POS/lemmatizer/parse/stem/spellcheck errors, small manual validation sample, and exact-span matching choice could all undermine per-type metric validity (implicit assumptions).

strengths.title: Clear chain from method to diagnostic utility
strengths.description: The paper logically connects alignment + deterministic classification to enabling per-error-type evaluation, and demonstrates the diagnostic payoff by analysing CoNLL-2014 systems.
evidence: Sections 2–4: pipeline described and then applied to all CoNLL-2014 outputs producing Tables 5–8 and qualitative summaries.

strengths.title: Dataset-independence and transparency of classifier
strengths.description: Rule-based deterministic taxonomy avoids dataset-specific training biases and supports interpretability of label assignments.
evidence: Section 3: motivation for rule-based approach; Section 3.1 lists preprocessing features used; Section 3.2 explains M/R/U tiers.

strengths.title: Manual expert validation included
strengths.description: Human expert ratings (5 raters, κfree reported) provide qualitative evidence that predicted labels are reasonable in typical cases.
evidence: Section 3.3: Table 3 with per-rater distributions and reported κfree = 0.724.

concerns.title: Limited quantitative evaluation of alignment quality on target data
concerns.description: The pipeline depends critically on the adopted Felice et al. (2016) alignment, but the manuscript does not quantify alignment precision/recall or types of boundary errors specifically on CoNLL-2014 system outputs; reliance on prior reported 80–85 F1 is insufficient to guarantee performance on noisy system hypotheses.
evidence: SHARED_ANALYSIS: Felice et al. (2016) 80-85 F1 cited, but no new alignment error breakdown for CoNLL-2014.
Section 2 states adoption of Felice et al.; no in-paper alignment evaluation provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate alignment accuracy on a stratified sample of CoNLL-2014 sentences by comparing automatic spans to human-annotated spans (compute precision/recall/F1), and report error types (split/merge/shift) and their frequency.

concerns.title: Small and potentially non-representative manual validation sample
concerns.description: The manual classifier evaluation uses 200 edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL) rated by 5 experts; this sample may underrepresent rare/complex edit types and boundary-induced misclassifications that would affect per-type metrics at scale.
evidence: Section 3.3: describes 200-edit sample and aggregated ratings.
SHARED_ANALYSIS flags small sample size as limiting generalisability.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Increase the manual sample size stratified by error type, edit size (single vs multi-token), and source (references vs hypotheses); report per-type Good/Acceptable/Bad rates and analyze disagreements.

concerns.title: Insufficient reporting of statistical testing details
concerns.description: The bootstrap test claiming no significant difference between auto and gold references is reported (1,000 iterations, p>.05) but lacks details (which metrics tested, exact p-values, confidence intervals, per-team or per-type results), preventing reproducibility and assessment of power.
evidence: Section 4.1: statement about bootstrap testing without full test reporting; Table 4 shows numeric differences but no CIs or p-values.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the tested metric(s), exact p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes per team; consider reporting per-type comparisons and statistical power analysis.

concerns.title: Potential sensitivity to preprocessing toolchain

evidence: Section 3.1 lists spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell; Section 3.3 notes POS errors explain many 'Bad' ratings.
SHARED_ANALYSIS recommends testing with alternate preprocessing tools.

Examples in Section 4.1 (have eating → has eaten vs have→has + eating→eaten).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a sensitivity analysis comparing exact matching with alternative matching strategies (e.g., fuzzy span overlap, semantic equivalence heuristics, or allowing span decomposition matching) and report how per-team and per-type scores shift.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a deterministic pipeline to (a) extract edit spans from original/corrected sentence pairs using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) and merging rules, and (b) assign dataset-agnostic error-type labels via a rule-based classifier relying only on automatic markup (POS, lemma, stem, dependency parse, spellchecking). The authors evaluate label appropriateness via a small manual rating (200 edits, 5 expert raters) and apply the pipeline to re-annotate CoNLL-2014 system outputs and references, enabling per-error-type precision/recall/F0.5 analysis and comparisons to M2 scoring. Major methodological claims are: labels are broadly appropriate (>95% Good/Acceptable across raters), auto-processing of references yields statistically indistinguishable aggregate results from gold-based M2 evaluation (bootstrap, 1,000 iterations), and the resulting per-type analysis reveals meaningful complementary strengths across systems. Key assumptions include sufficient alignment quality, robustness of the NLP toolchain on learner and system outputs, representativeness of the small manual sample, and that strict span+correction matching is an adequate evaluation criterion. Evidence is strongest for the feasibility of end-to-end processing and for illustrative diagnostic value; gaps remain in large-scale quantification of alignment/classifier errors by type, sensitivity analyses to preprocessing tool versions, full reporting of statistical tests (per-team p-values/effect sizes), and robustness of per-type claims to alignment/tagging failure modes.
logical_argument_graph: Step 1: Problem — system outputs lack error-type annotations, preventing per-type analysis.

Step 2: Solution architecture — use linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) to extract edits; apply deterministic rule-based classifier using automatic markup to assign error-type codes.
Step 3: Taxonomy — define 25 base token types, extendable with M/R/U operation prefixes yielding up to 55 codes for multi-granular evaluation.

Step 4: Validation of labels — perform small-scale manual evaluation (200 edits, 5 expert raters) to judge appropriateness (Good/Acceptable/Bad), reporting overall 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, κfree=0.724.

Step 5: Reprocessing references — run alignment+classifier on gold references to ensure hypothesis/reference comparability; bootstrap test (1,000 iterations) finds no significant aggregate differences vs gold/M2.

Step 6: Application — auto-annotate all CoNLL-2014 hypotheses and auto references; compute per-type P/R/F0.5 and conduct system-level diagnostic analysis (operation tier, detailed types, multi-token edits, detection vs correction).

Step 7: Interpretation — differences across systems (MT vs classifiers vs rules) reflect complementary strengths; pipeline enables previously infeasible per-type evaluation and diagnostic granularity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a deterministic, dataset-agnostic pipeline to (a) extract edit spans between original and corrected sentences using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (adopted from Felice et al., 2016) and (b) classify those edits into a compact taxonomy (25 base types, 55 with operation prefixes) using only automatic mark-up (POS, lemma, stem, dependency parse, spellcheck). The authors validate label appropriateness via a small manual rating (200 edits, 5 expert raters; 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, κfree=0.724) and demonstrate application by auto-annotating all CoNLL-2014 system outputs and reprocessed gold references, enabling edit-level matching (identical span+correction) and per-error-type precision/recall/F0.5 analyses across systems. They argue auto-reprocessing of references makes auto-vs-gold evaluation comparable (bootstrap test, 1,000 iterations, p>.05) and that their approach yields more conservative, arguably less inflated scores than M2 because it fixes edit spans rather than dynamically selecting boundaries. The contribution is an operational toolchain, a pragmatic taxonomy with M/R/U tiers, and an empirical diagnostic analysis of CoNLL-2014 systems. The work is incremental relative to prior edit-extraction and classifier-based efforts, but provides practical unification (alignment+deterministic typing) and the first full per-error-type system comparison on CoNLL-2014.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: system outputs are unannotated so per-error-type evaluation across systems is infeasible.
Step 1: Use linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) with merging rules to extract edit spans between original and corrected sentences (Section 2).

Step 2: Apply an entirely rule-based classifier using automatic token markup (spaCy POS/lemma/dep, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) to assign error-type codes from a compact taxonomy (Section 3, 3.1, 3.2).
Small-scale validation: ask expert raters to judge appropriateness of predicted labels on 200 edits; result: >95% Good/Acceptable and κfree=0.724 (Section 3.3).
Operational decision: reprocess gold references using the same pipeline as hypotheses to avoid span/segmentation mismatches and enable direct edit comparison (Section 4.1).
Empirical application: annotate all CoNLL-2014 outputs, compute per-team and per-type P/R/F0.5 using strict span+correction matching, and compare patterns across systems (Sections 4.2–4.6).

Claimed outcomes: auto-annotation produces qualitatively acceptable labels, reprocessed references are comparable to gold in aggregate, and the per-type breakdown reveals complementary system strengths/weaknesses (e.g., MT better at multi-token/noun; classifiers better at verb-form/orthography).

strengths.title: Transparent and deterministic labeling decisions
strengths.description: Rule-based classification makes the assignment process explainable and reproducible—useful for diagnostics and error analysis.
evidence: Section 3 emphasizes determinism and the ability to 'determine precisely why an edit was assigned to a particular error category.'

concerns.title: Small and possibly unrepresentative manual evaluation sample
concerns.description: Classifier appropriateness is validated on only 200 edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL-2014) rated by 5 experts; this sample may not capture rarer or more complex edit types and may bias the reported >95% Good/Acceptable figure.
evidence: Section 3.3: describes 200-edit sample and aggregated ratings; shared analysis flags small-sample limitation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Increase manual validation size stratified by error type and edit size (single-token vs multi-token), report per-type Good/Acceptable rates and sample selection criteria; provide confusion breakdown for 'Bad' cases.

concerns.title: Insufficient quantification of alignment errors on system outputs
concerns.description: The alignment component is assumed to perform well based on prior work, but the paper lacks a new quantitative evaluation of span extraction accuracy specifically on CoNLL-2014 system hypotheses, which may differ from training/other corpora.
evidence: Section 2 cites Felice et al. (2016) 80–85 F1 but does not present a direct alignment evaluation on the CoNLL-2014 hypotheses used in this study.
Shared analysis notes alignment errors could propagate into per-type metrics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report alignment precision/recall or F1 on a held-out human-annotated sample of CoNLL-2014 hypothesis-reference pairs (including system outputs) and characterize typical merge/split errors.

concerns.title: Heavy dependence on upstream NLP toolchain not tested
concerns.description: Rules rely on POS, lemma, parse, stemming and spellcheck produced by specific tool versions (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster, Hunspell). The paper acknowledges POS-tagging errors cause many 'Bad' labels but does not quantify sensitivity to tool choice or tagging accuracy on learner data.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists toolchain; Section 3.3 attributes many 'Bad' ratings to POS tagger mistakes.
Shared analysis recommends ablation with different tool versions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablation experiments swapping core tools (modern spaCy/POS tagger, alternative stemmer, newer spellcheck dictionaries) and report per-type changes; provide error correlation between upstream tool mistakes and classification errors.

concerns.title: Strict span+correction matching may undercount semantically equivalent edits
concerns.description: Requiring identical span and correction for a true positive will penalize equivalent corrections with different segmentation/decomposition (e.g., single multi-token edit vs two token-level edits), biasing F scores and per-type recall.
evidence: Section 4.1 notes examples where M2 decompositions yield different match counts; authors discuss M2’s dynamic boundary selection and its effects.
Shared analysis points out lack of formal sensitivity analysis to span granularity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include an analysis of partial/fuzzy matching (e.g., token overlap thresholds, semantic equivalence heuristics) to quantify how strict matching affects P/R by edit size and by type; report alternative scores under relaxed matching.

concerns.title: Incomplete reporting of statistical testing details
concerns.description: The bootstrap test claiming no significant difference between auto and gold references (1,000 iterations, p>.05) lacks details: which metric was tested, exact p-values, confidence intervals, and per-team/per-type outcomes.
evidence: Section 4.1: authors state they validated equivalence using bootstrap testing but do not provide full test statistics or p-values.
Table 4 shows aggregate numbers but no test details.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full statistical reporting: tested metric(s), bootstrapped confidence intervals, p-values per team and optionally per major error category; include effect size estimates.

concerns.title: Incremental novelty with limited conceptual departure
concerns.description: Most components reuse or adapt prior ideas (Felice et al. alignment; Swanson/Xue classifier motivations); the novelty lies in integrating alignment + deterministic labeling and applying it at scale for per-type system diagnostics rather than in a fundamentally new algorithmic approach.
evidence: Section 2 credits Felice et al. (2016) for alignment; Section 3 states inspiration from Swanson and Yamangil (2012) observations about POS-driven types.
Comparable literature includes ML classifiers and M2-based evaluation but not an identical deterministic pipeline producing full CoNLL-2014 per-type analyses.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify novelty claims explicitly: state which parts are reused/adapted and which elements (e.g., taxonomy design, reprocessing-of-references idea, full shared-task per-type analysis) are novel contributions.

uncertainty_flags: Manual evaluation sample small (200 edits) — uncertain representativeness across error types and edit sizes.
Alignment reliability on noisy system hypotheses is not directly measured in this paper—risk of propagated span errors.
Classifier performance may degrade with alternative preprocessing tools or updated versions — toolchain sensitivity untested.
Bootstrap equivalence claim (auto vs. gold) lacks per-team p-values and effect sizes—equivalence uncertain for subsets or specific types.
Strict span+correction matching may systematically penalize systems that produce semantically equivalent but differently segmented edits (multi-token vs decomposed edits).
alternative_interpretations: High Good/Acceptable ratings could be inflated because raters were instructed to ignore boundary issues, so some classification 'success' may mask alignment problems or mis-segmentation.

Aggregate equivalence between auto and gold references might hold overall but mask per-type systematic differences where alignment or classification errors disproportionately affect certain categories.

Apparent system strengths (MT vs classifiers) might partly reflect differential susceptibility to alignment/typing errors (e.g., multi-token edits better captured by the alignment approach), not purely algorithmic competence.
transparency_notes: Tool release is promised but no URL, license, or artifact version is included in the paper; reproduction requires tool availability and exact toolchain versions.
Key statistical tests (bootstrap) are described but lack full reporting (metric used, exact p-values, confidence intervals), limiting verifiability of the 'no significant difference' claim.

Implementation details of the rule set (full rule list, decision order, resolution of conflicting rules) are not fully enumerated in the main text or appendix; publishing the rule code would aid reproducibility.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While many building blocks (linguistically-informed alignment, POS-driven classification) are present in the literature, the novelty is in their combination and operationalization to auto-annotate system outputs at scale and produce the first complete per-error-type analysis of CoNLL-2014. Novelty here is primarily practical and applied; it does not imply methodological novelty or validity in all settings.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If alignment accuracy on system hypotheses remains close to the cited 80–85 F1 (or better) across edit sizes, then downstream error-typing and per-type metrics will be reliable.
If upstream NLP tools (POS/tagger/lemmatizer/spellchecker) perform robustly on learner and system-generated text, rule-based classification will maintain high appropriateness.
If manual validation is expanded and shows similar Good/Acceptable rates across rarer and multi-token edits, the pipeline's generalisability is supported.
If ablation with alternative preprocessing tools yields consistent per-type results, the approach is robust to toolchain choices.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The methodology adapts established alignment and POS-driven classification ideas; the novelty is in integrating them into a deterministic, dataset-agnostic pipeline and applying it at scale for diagnostic per-type evaluation, a gap in prior work.
evidence: Use of Felice et al. (2016) alignment and inspiration from Swanson & Yamangil (2012) for POS-based typing; authors apply pipeline to full CoNLL-2014 outputs producing novel analyses.
uncertainty_flags: Degree to which integration yields robust per-type metrics depends on alignment and upstream tool accuracy, which are not fully quantified here.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Rule-based deterministic typing avoids dataset-specific training bias, but relies on automatic markup which may vary across datasets and languages; generality requires further empirical validation.
evidence: Section 3 emphasizes dataset-independence; toolchain is specified but robustness tests across corpora or tool variants are not provided.
uncertainty_flags: No cross-dataset experiments or toolchain ablations presented.

novelty_lenses.verdict: high practical value if released, reproducibility contingent
novelty_lenses.rationale: If the tool and full rule set are published, the pipeline would be immediately useful for error analysis and diagnostics across systems; current reproducibility is hampered by missing artifact URLs and incomplete statistical reporting.
evidence: Paper declares tool will be released; detailed per-system tables show utility.
uncertainty_flags: Tool not yet available in the paper; rule code and test harness needed to reproduce results.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper does not present fundamentally new theoretical constructs; instead it offers an applied framework and taxonomy balanced for practicality.
evidence: Taxonomy design rationale and rule-based mapping to POS/operation tiers; no novel learning algorithms or formal theoretical claims.
uncertainty_flags: The taxonomy design choices could still influence downstream analyses and deserve formal validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately to highly confident in the assessment that the paper is an incremental, practically valuable contribution (integration + scale application) but that several methodological gaps (alignment evaluation on system outputs, small manual sample, toolchain sensitivity, and incomplete statistical reporting) limit the strength of claims about generalisability and equivalence to gold references. The interval reflects uncertainty due to missing empirical validations and artifact availability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a two-stage, fully deterministic pipeline to auto-annotate unlabelled GEC outputs: (1) extract edit spans using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016 method + merging rules) and (2) assign dataset-agnostic error-type labels via a rule-based classifier relying only on automatic markup (POS, lemma, stem, parse, spellchecking). The authors define a compact taxonomy (25 base types; up to 55 with M/R/U prefixes), validate label appropriateness with a small manual rating (200 edits, 5 experts; 86.3% Good, 10% Acceptable, κfree=0.724), reprocess CoNLL-2014 references with the same pipeline and argue that evaluation using auto-annotated references is statistically indistinguishable from gold-based M2 scoring (bootstrap 1,000 iterations, p>.05). They then apply the pipeline across all CoNLL-2014 system outputs to produce the first large-scale per-error-type diagnostic analysis, reporting complementary system strengths/weaknesses and multi-token/edit-size effects. Core claims: dataset-independence and transparency of rule-based approach; high qualitative appropriateness of labels; comparability of auto-annotated evaluation to gold-reference evaluation; new per-error-type insights on CoNLL-2014 teams.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Existing GEC system outputs are unlabelled for error type → Need: method to automatically produce per-error-type annotations (Introduction).
P2: Linguistically-enhanced alignment approximates human edits well (Felice et al., 2016: 80–85 F1) → Use as edit-extraction component (Section 2).
P3: Most error categories are characterisable by POS/operation cues → Construct deterministic rules using automatic markup (Section 3).
P4: Deterministic rules produce transparent, dataset-agnostic labels → Advantage vs. learned classifiers which require corpus-specific training (Section 3).
P5: Manual rating of a sample shows high appropriateness (86.3% Good; κfree=0.724) → Empirical support that labels are meaningful in context (Section 3.3).

P6: Reprocessing references with same automatic pipeline and bootstrap testing shows no significant difference vs. gold M2 evaluation → Claim that auto-annotated references are a fair proxy for gold (Section 4.1, Table 4).
C1: The proposed pipeline can automatically annotate unlabelled GEC outputs reliably enough to support per-error-type evaluation (synthesis of P1–P6).
P7: Applying pipeline to CoNLL-2014 yields per-system per-type metrics revealing complementary strengths (Section 4.2–4.5) → Demonstration of utility.
C2: This enables new diagnostic analyses (multi-token, operation tiers, detection vs correction) that were previously infeasible at scale.

identified_claims.claim_text: Edit spans between original and corrected sentences are automatically extracted using a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) with merging rules, which approximates human edits effectively and is used as the edit-extraction component in this work.
evidence: Section 2: use of Felice et al. (2016) linguistically-enhanced alignment and merging rules.
Manuscript text: "This approach ultimately proved most effective at approximating human edits in several datasets (80-85 F1), and so we use it in the present study."
uncertainty_flags: Reported 80–85 F1 is from Felice et al. (2016) and not a re-evaluation of the alignment on the CoNLL-2014 / system hypothesis corpus within this paper.
No quantitative breakdown is provided of alignment errors (split/merged spans) on the actual system outputs used for analyses.

identified_claims.claim_text: A deterministic, dataset-independent, rule-based classifier that uses only automatic mark-up (POS, lemma, stem, dependency parse, spellcheck) can assign error-type labels to extracted edits without requiring annotated training data.
evidence: Section 3: description of writing rules based on POS and insert/delete/substitute distinctions and additional rules for non-POS types.
Section 3.1: concrete toolchain: spaCy v1.6, Lancaster Stemmer, Hunspell GB-large.
uncertainty_flags: Extent of rule coverage and failure modes for rarer, ambiguous, or noisy learner-language edits is not exhaustively quantified.
Dependency on specific preprocessing tool versions and configurations is acknowledged but not empirically tested for robustness.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed framework defines 25 (plus operation-tier prefixes leading to 55 possible codes) error types, which can be prefixed with operation tiers M:, R:, U: to allow varying granularity of evaluation.
evidence: Section 3.2: "The complete list of 25 error types... can be prefixed with ‘M:’, ‘R:’ or ‘U:’..."
Appendix A / Table 9: enumerates valid combinations and states 55 total possible error types.
uncertainty_flags: Taxonomy choices are pragmatic and might conflate distinct phenomena (modal vs tense); no inter-annotator taxonomic validation is provided.
Impacts of taxonomy granularity on classifier confusion by type are not quantified at scale.

identified_claims.claim_text: In a small-scale manual evaluation, five GEC researchers rated 200 randomly chosen automatically predicted edits (100 FCE-test, 100 CoNLL-2014) and each rater considered at least 95% of predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable'; overall distribution across raters was 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad, with κfree = 0.724.
evidence: Section 3.3: description of raters, rating scheme and instruction to ignore boundary oddities.
Table 3: per-rater percentages and reported κfree.
uncertainty_flags: Sample size (200 edits) is limited relative to full CoNLL-2014 system outputs and may not represent rarer, complex edits.
Raters were told to ignore boundary issues; hence some boundary-driven misclassifications may be underreported.

identified_claims.claim_label: auto reprocessing references matches gold evaluation
identified_claims.claim_text: Reprocessing gold reference edits automatically (running alignment+classifier on references) and then evaluating hypotheses against these auto-annotated references yields overall scores that are not significantly different from evaluation using gold references and standard M2 scoring (bootstrap testing, 1000 iterations, p > .05).
identified_claims.section_anchor: Section 4.1 (Gold Reference vs. Auto Reference), Table 4
evidence: Section 4.1: rationale for reprocessing references and statement of bootstrap testing showing no significant difference.
Table 4: side-by-side M2 and 'Our Approach' scores for gold and auto references for each team.
uncertainty_flags: Test details are underreported: which metric(s) tested, per-team p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes are not provided.
Aggregate non-significance might mask per-type or per-team meaningful differences.

identified_claims.claim_label: first per-error-type analysis of CoNLL-2014 systems
identified_claims.claim_text: Auto-annotating hypotheses and references enables a detailed per-error-type analysis of all CoNLL-2014 system outputs, revealing complementary strengths and weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT systems better at multi-token and certain noun errors; classifiers better at some verb-form and orthography errors).
evidence: Section 4: application to all teams and presentation of per-team per-type P/R/F0.5 tables (Tables 5–8) and narrative on system strengths.
Section 4.5 Table 8: multi-token edit performance showing MT systems higher on multi-token edits.
uncertainty_flags: Per-type findings depend on quality of automatic alignment and classification; propagation of upstream errors could bias the per-type comparison.
Statistical significance of per-type inter-system differences is not consistently reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: The automatic annotation tool used in this study will be released with the paper.
evidence: Abstract and sections explicitly state: "The tool we use to do this will be released with this paper."
uncertainty_flags: No URL, artifact metadata, license, or reproducibility instructions are present in the manuscript; actual availability must be verified externally.

strengths.title: Practical, transparent dataset-agnostic annotation pipeline
strengths.description: A fully deterministic rule-based classifier combined with a linguistically-informed aligner provides an interpretable method to annotate system outputs without labelled data.
evidence: Section 3: rules based on POS/lemma/operation only; transparency emphasized: "always possible to determine precisely why an edit was assigned..."
Section 2: adoption of a linguistically-enhanced alignment approach (Felice et al., 2016).

strengths.title: Concrete taxonomy with multi-granularity operation tiers
strengths.description: A compact taxonomy (25 types; up to 55 with M/R/U prefixes) enables flexible evaluation slices (token type, operation type, or both).
evidence: Section 3.2 and Appendix A Table 9 enumerating valid combinations and operation-tier design.
Examples in Section 3.2 showing trade-offs (modal vs. tense).

strengths.title: Demonstrated application at scale (CoNLL-2014)
strengths.description: Applying the pipeline across all CoNLL-2014 system outputs produced extensive per-type diagnostic tables and novel observations about system complementarity.
evidence: Section 4: Tables 5–8 and narrative summarising CAMB, CUUI, AMU performance differences and multi-token edit analysis (Table 8).

strengths.title: Human qualitative validation (expert ratings)
strengths.description: Manual evaluation by five GEC researchers shows a high proportion of predicted types deemed Good or Acceptable, lending qualitative support to label appropriateness.
evidence: Section 3.3, Table 3: overall distribution 86.3% Good, 10% Acceptable; κfree=0.724 reported.

concerns.title: Limited and potentially unrepresentative manual evaluation
concerns.description: Classifier appropriateness is judged on only 200 edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL-2014), which is small relative to the full corpus and may bias the apparent high 'Good/Acceptable' rates toward common or easy edits.
evidence: Section 3.3: sample size = 200; raters instructed to ignore boundary issues.
SHARED_ANALYSIS uncertainty: small manual evaluation sample limits generalisability.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand manual evaluation to a stratified sample covering rarer error types, multi-token edits, and cases where tagger/alignment disagreement is likely; report per-type appropriateness, and include examples of 'Bad' classifications with root-cause annotations (POS vs alignment vs rule coverage).

concerns.title: Insufficient quantification of alignment/span errors on target data
concerns.description: The Felice et al. (2016) alignment F1 is cited, but the manuscript does not re-evaluate alignment quality specifically on CoNLL-2014 system hypotheses or on different system outputs; boundary errors could drive downstream label mismatches and evaluation bias.
evidence: Section 2: adoption of Felice et al. (2016) results (80–85 F1) without per-corpus re-evaluation.
Assumption A1 in shared analysis: alignment adequacy is critical but not empirically quantified here.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate alignment precision/recall on a held-out human-aligned subset of CoNLL-2014 (including multi-token cases and system outputs) and report how alignment errors propagate to label and evaluation errors (confusion matrix between human edits and auto-extracted edits).

concerns.title: Dependence on preprocessing toolchain without robustness analysis
concerns.description: The rule-based classifier relies on spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, and Hunspell; POS tagging and spellcheck mistakes are cited as the main source of 'Bad' ratings, but no systematic sensitivity analysis is presented.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists specific toolchain; Section 3.3 notes POS tagger errors explain many 'Bad' labels.
Assumption A2: operational dependence on automatic tools is a risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablation/robustness experiments swapping POS taggers/stemmers/spellcheckers (or modern versions), report per-type label stability, and quantify how often label decisions change due to preprocessing variations.

concerns.title: Underreported statistical testing and potential masking of per-type differences
concerns.description: Bootstrap testing claiming 'no significant difference' between auto and gold references is reported without per-team/per-type p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes; aggregate non-significance may hide meaningful discrepancies for specific types or systems.
evidence: Section 4.1: "bootstrap significance testing (1,000 iterations, p > .05)" without more detail.
SHARED_ANALYSIS notes missing test statistic details and per-type reporting.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide test details (metric tested, null hypothesis, resampling unit), per-team and per-type p-values and confidence intervals, and report effect sizes; consider reporting where auto- vs gold-reference differences exceed practically meaningful thresholds.

concerns.title: Strict span+correction matching may undercount semantically equivalent edits
concerns.description: Evaluation matches require identical spans and corrections, which penalises equivalent corrections split differently (e.g., one multi-token vs two single-token edits) and may bias against systems that segment edits divergently.
evidence: Section 4: description that TP requires same span and correction; multiple examples and discussion of M2's dynamic boundary strategy.
Shared analysis assumption A5: strict matching can undercount semantically equivalent corrections.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report sensitivity analyses using alternate matching strategies (fuzzy span overlap, semantic equivalence, allow merged/split tolerance) and quantify changes in per-type and overall scores; explicitly compare to M2 outputs for representative ambiguous cases.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides the alignment algorithm this paper adopts; this manuscript applies it to full CoNLL-2014 outputs and pairs it with a novel deterministic taxonomy/classifier.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Section 2 cites Felice et al. (2016) and quotes 80–85 F1.

comparable_works.relevance: Early attempt at edit extraction and error-typing using Levenshtein-based alignment and classifier-based typing.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Swanson & Yamangil used ML classifiers and merging heuristics; current paper departs by using deterministic rules to aim for dataset-independence and transparency.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Section 2 and 3 reference Swanson and Yamangil (2012).

comparable_works.relevance: Improved merging prediction via max-entropy classifier; relevant to edit-merging decisions.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: They use learned merging decisions whereas the present work relies on deterministic merging rules informed by linguistic cues.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 references Xue & Hwa (2014).
